opus-1.method: The method learns from trusted rewards and favors shorter answers among those receiving the highest reward for each prompt. It ignores task reward on ordinary prompts and uses them only to penalize answers that the original monitor flags. Avoiding hacks that the monitor misses therefore depends on what the model learns from trusted examples and the preference for shorter answers. The algorithm trains adapters across the model’s linear layers and stops when trusted reward plateaus or the 80-minute limit expires.

process.lead: Adding imitation lowered all three pilot scores.
process.text: The agent therefore removed the imitation step and returned to the earlier objective.

process.lead: Later validation experiments did not improve on the selected method.
process.text: After evaluating the earlier method in a full run, the agent retained it when subsequent variants failed to improve the tasks it tested.

opus-2.method: The method learns task performance from trusted rewards and uses ordinary prompts only to penalize answers that the original monitor flags. It also penalizes answer length on trusted prompts and uses paired comparisons of trusted rewards to choose a sampling temperature after training. The algorithm incorporates that temperature into the model’s final normalization weights, so the model generates answers with the chosen setting under the grader’s standard decoding procedure. During training, smaller batches limit the number of tokens in memory.

opus-3.method: The method trains an additional detector on monitor labels and uses its predictions to penalize suspected hacks during RL, including answers that the original monitor does not flag. It learns the task from trusted rewards and selects checkpoints on trusted validation prompts. The algorithm waits until it has enough flagged and unflagged examples to fit the detector and rejects fits with non-finite values.

It learns the task from trusted rewards and uses ordinary prompts only for monitor penalties, reserving one fifth of trusted prompts for validation. Both training and checkpoint selection rely on the original monitor. The final model uses temperature 0.5, and the agent extended the final version’s training allowance without separately evaluating that version on the dev set.

opus-5.method: The algorithm augments the monitor with a probe trained on the base model’s activations. Before policy training, it labels roughly 2,048 sampled answers with the monitor and uses them to initialize the probe. Policy training then combines trusted rewards with monitor and probe penalties. Trusted validation selects the checkpoint, and temperature calibration adjusts the deployed policy.

opus-6.method: The algorithm uses trusted task rewards and penalizes ordinary answers when the monitor flags them or their reward exceeds its estimated clean-reward range. It scales penalties to the observed reward range and favors brevity among the best answers. Validation selects a checkpoint and deployment temperature, but does not stop training: the final version trains to its step or time limit.

opus-7.method: The algorithm trains with GRPO on trusted rewards and uses ordinary prompts only to penalize monitor flags. It reserves trusted prompts before training for checkpoint selection, early stopping, and temperature calibration. Excluding these prompts from training makes validation measure performance on unseen trusted examples rather than memorization of the training pool.

opus-8.method: The algorithm trains a linear reward predictor on token n-grams from trusted answers. On ordinary prompts, it caps the environment reward at this predictor’s estimate, then subtracts monitor and length penalties. GRPO uses these rewards to update the policy. After training, it selects a temperature from 1.0, 0.8, 0.6, and 0.4 using trusted prompts and folds it into the policy weights. Deployment requires no reward predictor.

sol-1.method: The algorithm samples several answers per trusted prompt and imitates the highest-reward answer that the monitor does not flag, breaking ties in favor of shorter answers. It trains query and value adapters, selects its checkpoint on separate trusted validation prompts, and stops after validation stalls. It uses neither pseudo-labels nor gradients from ordinary prompts.

sol-2.method: The algorithm imitates high-reward trusted answers and updates adapters on all linear layers. A separate trusted audit set supports paired checkpoint comparisons. A frozen reference policy measures progress: only a statistically significant utility gain or shortening resets early-stopping patience. This separates the decision to continue training from the decision to replace the best checkpoint.

sol-3.method: The method combines RL on trusted rewards with imitation of successful answers that the monitor does not flag. The RL update subtracts ten times the monitor flag from trusted reward, and the imitation step chooses the shortest unflagged answer among those receiving the highest reward for each prompt. A small reward bonus also favors shorter successful answers, while a KL penalty limits changes from the base model. The algorithm relies on the original monitor and stops training when trusted reward plateaus or the run reaches a step or time limit.

process.text: Teaching the model to end its answers on ordinary prompts hurt performance, and removing that loss recovered sorting performance. The agent kept the earlier method because the later candidates lacked a stronger complete evaluation.

After step 50, it also imitates answers on ordinary prompts when at least 75% of sampled answers agree. This consensus supplies pseudo-labels without reading their task reward. The final version adds token-bounded batches, rollout limits, and a runtime guard to make the selected method finish reliably.

sol-5.method: The algorithm imitates the best trusted answers only when they meet a moving reward threshold. It replays qualifying examples and reduces the probability of monitor-flagged answers. Once competence reaches the configured threshold and reward progress saturates, it freezes a teacher, greedily generates trusted answers, and imitates only unflagged answers at the reward frontier. This final stage concentrates the policy on successful outputs.

sol-6.method: The algorithm imitates the shortest highest-reward unflagged answer for each trusted prompt. It also trains on preference pairs that favor unflagged answers over monitor-flagged answers from both trusted and ordinary prompts. A persistent replay buffer retains these pairs and their original reference margins, allowing later updates to revisit earlier safety examples.

sol-7.method: The algorithm combines quality-filtered imitation of trusted answers with trusted-reward GRPO. It keeps successful answers in replay and computes a guard gradient from completed, nonempty answers at the highest trusted reward observed so far. When the RL gradient opposes this guard, it removes the conflicting component before the update. Trusted validation selects the checkpoint and stopping point. The method also uses base-model and frozen-teacher proposals and delays abstention until its competence gate permits it.

sol-8.method: The algorithm combines a trusted-reward policy gradient with imitation of the shortest answers at its current reward frontier. For a monitor-flagged answer, it finds the closest unflagged answer to the same prompt and penalizes only the differing tokens. It also collects flagged negatives from ordinary prompts without reading their rewards, then replays these examples during training.

astra-8.method: The method trains a detector to identify likely hacks that the monitor misses, then penalizes answers that either the detector or monitor flags. These penalties push the language model to produce those answers less often. The model learns the task from trusted rewards, while ordinary prompts provide additional examples for training the detector. The detector uses frozen base-model activations for the prompt and answer and learns from monitor labels and comparisons between answers to the same trusted prompt. The RL update subtracts a leave-one-out baseline from task rewards but applies safety penalties directly so that equal penalties do not cancel. The model also imitates high-reward answers that pass both checks. After training, it generates answers without consulting the detector.
